steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on formally verifying generic railway interlocking logic using Dafny together with parameterized model checking. Explain what interlocking systems are, the industrial context we work in, what we tried before and why it fell short, and what this paper proposes.

- Context: RFI framework for designing interlocking logics

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Interlocking systems
  - complex, safety-critical; control devices in a railway station
  - main function: safe routes for trains between points in the station
  - devices on a route (semaphores, switches, level crossing) operated properly; mutual exclusion between interfering routes
  - abstractly: articulated mutual exclusion protocol = interlocking logic
- Context
  - formal approach for reliability and integrity, complementing standard validation and certification
  - RFI (manages Italian railways network): in-house framework to design interlocking logics and support development (cite)
  - goal: computer-based, beyond relay-based interlocking technology
  - controlled natural language -> model-based IDE for signaling engineers; well-structured, unambiguous spec
  - logic is generic: any station in a class, not a single station
  - spec -> SysML model -> executable code
  - user defines station configuration (e.g. Trento): number of components, interactions
  - configured code tested in closed loop with yard simulator (trains, physical devices)
- Previous attempts (cite)
  - software model checking on code configured for a specific station: scalability barrier (instantiated model too big); results only for that station
  - generic logic without instantiation: SMT-based, quantified invariants; large formulae, hard to reason about, no structure
- Our approach
  - object-oriented features of Dafny; high-level, natural framework for generic interlocking logics
  - artificial but representative case study; model in Dafny, verify generic properties
  - more automation: template-based simple invariants + parameterized model checker for complex, problem specific invariants
  - promising results; open challenges for scalability

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Interlocking systems are complex systems that are safety-critical and control the operation of the devices in a railway station. Their main function is to create safe routes for trains from different points in the station. For this, the devices that insist upon a given route (e.g. semaphores, switches, level crossing) have to be operated properly, and mutual exclusion between routes that interfere has to be ensured. At a high level of abstraction, you can think of an interlocking system as implementing a very articulated mutual exclusion protocol, which we call interlocking logic.

In this paper we look at using a formal approach to ensure that their operations are reliable and keep their integrity, as a complement to the standard validation and certification techniques. The context is an ongoing activity of RFI, the company that manages the Italian railways network, which aims to develop an in-house framework for designing interlocking logics and supporting the development of interlocking systems. One goal of this framework is to develop computer-based interlocking, so as to go beyond the current relay-based interlocking technology. The interlocking logic is described starting from a high-level controlled natural language, and a model-based Integrated Development Environment helps the railways signaling engineers to specify the interlocking logic in a way that is well-structured and semantically unambiguous. The interlocking logic is generic, which is interesting, because it describes the procedures without referring to a single, given station, and instead it applies to any station in a given class. The specification is then translated into a SysML model, and from that it is compiled into executable code. After that the user can define a specific station configuration (e.g. the station of the city of Trento), with the exact number of components and how they interact. Once configured, the code can be tested in closed loop integration with a yard simulator that models how trains and physical devices behave.

- Previous attempts
  - software model checking on code for a specific station: scalability barrier, huge instantiated model; results only valid for that station
  - generic logic without instantiation: SMT-based, quantified invariants; large formulae, hard to reason about, no structure
- Our approach
  - Dafny's object-oriented features; high-level natural framework for generic interlocking logics
  - artificial but representative case study; modeling in Dafny, verifying generic properties
  - automation: template-based simple invariants + parameterized model checker for complex invariants
  - promising; open challenges for scalability

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Interlocking systems are complex systems that are safety-critical and control the operation of the devices in a railway station. Their main function is to create safe routes for trains from different points in the station. For this, the devices that insist upon a given route (e.g. semaphores, switches, level crossing) have to be operated properly, and mutual exclusion between routes that interfere has to be ensured. At a high level of abstraction, you can think of an interlocking system as implementing a very articulated mutual exclusion protocol, which we call interlocking logic.

In this paper we look at using a formal approach to ensure that their operations are reliable and keep their integrity, as a complement to the standard validation and certification techniques. The context is an ongoing activity of RFI, the company that manages the Italian railways network, which aims to develop an in-house framework for designing interlocking logics and supporting the development of interlocking systems. One goal of this framework is to develop computer-based interlocking, so as to go beyond the current relay-based interlocking technology. The interlocking logic is described starting from a high-level controlled natural language, and a model-based Integrated Development Environment helps the railways signaling engineers to specify the interlocking logic in a way that is well-structured and semantically unambiguous. The interlocking logic is generic, which is interesting, because it describes the procedures without referring to a single, given station, and instead it applies to any station in a given class. The specification is then translated into a SysML model, and from that it is compiled into executable code. After that the user can define a specific station configuration (e.g. the station of the city of Trento), with the exact number of components and how they interact. Once configured, the code can be tested in closed loop integration with a yard simulator that models how trains and physical devices behave.

Formally verifying the interlocking logic is a very important goal, and there have been several attempts in this direction. On one side, we tried to apply software model checking techniques to the code configured for a specific station. This approach ran into a scalability barrier, because the instantiated model was so large. More importantly, the verification results would only apply to that specific station. On the other side, we tried to verify the generic interlocking logic without instantiating it for a specific station. We followed an SMT-based approach that aims at finding quantified invariants. This gives large formulae that are difficult to reason about, because there is no proper structure.

Based on these experiences, we are now investigating a different approach, which uses the object-oriented features of Dafny to get a high-level and natural framework for tackling the verification of generic interlocking logics. We present a case study that is artificial but representative, showing how we intend to model the problem in Dafny and how we verify some generic properties. We hint that the verification can be made more automatic by combining template-based generation of simple invariants with a parameterized model checker that generates more complex, problem specific invariants. We think the results are quite promising and that the approach is worth investigating further. We also discuss the open challenges that we still need to solve to make the approach scalable.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Interlocking systems are complex, safety-critical systems controlling the operation of the devices in a railway station. Their main function is the creation of safe routes for trains from different points in the station. This requires that the devices insisting upon a given route (e.g. semaphores, switches, level crossing) are properly operated and that mutual exclusion between interfering routes is ensured. At a high level of abstraction, an interlocking system can be thought of as implementing a very articulated mutual exclusion protocol, which we refer to as interlocking logic.

In this paper, we investigate the use of a formal approach to ensure the reliability and integrity of their operations, as a complement to the standard validation and certification techniques. Our context is an ongoing activity of RFI (the company managing the Italian railways network), aiming to develop an in-house framework to design interlocking logics and support the development of interlocking systems [1,2]. One of the goals of this framework is to develop computer-based interlocking, in order to go beyond the current relay-based interlocking technology. Starting from a high-level controlled natural language to describe the interlocking logic, a model-based Integrated Development Environment supports the railways signaling engineers in specifying the interlocking logic in a well-structured and semantically unambiguous way. Interestingly, the interlocking logic is generic: it describes the procedures without reference to a single, given station, and applies instead to any station in a given class. The resulting specification is translated into a SysML model, and from there compiled into executable code. The user can then define a specific station configuration (e.g. the station of the city of Trento), detailing the exact number of components and their interactions. Once configured, the code can be tested in a closed loop integration with a yard simulator modeling the behavior of trains and physical devices.

Formally verifying the interlocking logic is a very important goal, and several attempts have been made in this direction [3,4]. On the one side, we attempted to apply software model checking techniques to the code configured for a specific station. This approach hit a scalability barrier, due to the sheer size of the instantiated model. Even more importantly, the verification results would apply to a specific station only. On the other side, we tried to tackle the verification of the generic interlocking logic without instantiating it for a specific station, following an SMT-based approach aimed at devising quantified invariants. This leads to large formulae that are difficult to reason about, due to the lack of a proper structure.

Based on these experiences, we are investigating an alternative approach that leverages the object-oriented features of Dafny to obtain a high-level and natural framework in which to tackle the verification of generic interlocking logics. We present an artificial but representative case study that shows how we intend to model the problem in Dafny, and show how we verify some generic properties. We hint that automation in the verification can be increased by combining template-based generation of simple invariants with the use of a parameterized model checker to generate more complex, problem specific invariants. We believe the results are quite promising and that the approach is worth investigating further. We discuss the open challenges that still need to be solved to make this approach scalable.
